parts: Only the best and the freshest raw material can guarantee good results in baking. The commonly used ingredients are flour, yeast, chemical raising agents, salt, cornflour, milk, cream, shortening agents, eggs, sugars, cocoa and chocolate, coffee, nuts, meat and poultry products, fresh and candied fruits, spices and aromatics, alcohol, food colours and essences. Depending on keeping quality, shelf life and storage temperature they are classified as: non-perishable (kept for more than a month at room temperature, e.g. flour, sugar, salt, spices, cocoa and coffee powders, colours, essences, canned products), perishable (kept a couple of days at the most at proper temperature, e.g. milk, cream, fresh fruits and vegetables, poultry and meat) and semi-perishable (need proper storage temperature but keep longer than perishables, e.g. butter and other fats, chocolates, opened tins, eggs).

Flour is the most important ingredient and is obtained by milling wheat. A wheat grain has bran, endosperm and germ; both bran and germ are removed during milling. Whole meal (whole wheat, 'atta') flour contains all parts of the grain; brown flour has the coarser bran removed and is used for brown bread; white flour ('maida') has most of the bran and germ removed; strong flour has a higher protein content and is used for breads, buns and patties; soft (weak) flour has more starch and less protein and is used for cakes, biscuits and pastries; self raising flour has the raising agent already mixed in. Yeast is a unicellular micro-organism of plant origin (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) which needs air, moisture, warmth and sugar to multiply and produce carbon dioxide that raises the dough. Fresh yeast is pale beige, firm but crumbly, with a pleasant fruity smell, is kept in a refrigerator for a couple of weeks (frozen for months) and gives better products; dried yeast is in granules, a little darker, sold in sachets, keeps for a few months in a cool cupboard (one month after opening) and is used in half the quantity because it is more concentrated. Chemical raising agents: baking powder (sodium bicarbonate, cream of tartar and a separator such as rice, potato or corn starch; the acid neutralises the left-over soda so no after taste is left), ammonium bicarbonate (gives ammonia gas that leaves an off taste) and baking soda (costs less, but the sodium carbonate residue leaves a bad taste and dark colour, so it suits only darker chocolate cakes).
Salt, milk, shortenings, eggs and sugars

Salt (sodium chloride) contains 40% sodium and 60% chlorine; it gives flavour, accentuates other flavours, has a stabilising effect on gluten, controls the speed of fermentation in yeast goods and helps retain moisture. Cornflour (from maize) is a thickening agent in custards and dilutes the strength of flour. Milk contains about 87% water and is a moistening and enriching agent; milk powder saves space and keeps well; condensed milk is made by evaporating water under vacuum. Cream is the fat portion (skimmed milk fat) of milk and must be refrigerated. Shortening agents: butter (made by churning milk, about 85% fat, pleasant aroma, store below 40 F), margarine (a cheaper butter substitute made from hydrogenated oils, no aroma), vanaspati ghee (hydrogenated oils with a grainy texture, less suitable for baked goods) and refined oil (liquid at room temperature, cannot be used for creaming, used for frying and greasing tins). After flour, eggs are the second structure forming material: white whisks easily and makes cakes lighter, yolk emulsifies and is used as a glaze. An average egg weighs 45-50 g; a fresh egg sinks in water and a stale one floats. Sugars: grain sugar (99% carbohydrate), castor sugar (finer, suitable for creaming), icing sugar (very fine powder for icing, glazes, dusting and almond paste), brown sugar (unrefined raw sugar for rich cakes), golden syrup (by-product of sugar refining, for ginger cakes), treacle (darker than golden syrup, for dark fruit cakes and Christmas pudding), honey, liquid glucose (made by boiling starch in water), milk sugar (lactose) and malt sugar (maltose). Cocoa powder is low in fat and has no sugar whereas chocolate has sugar, cocoa butter and milk added.

Light equipment: knives, scissors, graters, sieves, strainers, chopping boards, spoons, rolling pin, whisks, measuring jug, bowls, degchi, saucepan, karahi, turntable, cake dummies, lemon squeezer, pastry brush, weighing scale, sugar thermometer, biscuit cutters, piping bags and nozzles, cooling rack, trays, cake tins, moulds, Swiss roll tray, tartlet moulds, flan rings and baking trays. Heavy equipment: oven (gas, coal or electric), proving chamber, refrigerator, dough mixer, deep freezer, work tables, storage cabinet and gas burners. Ovens may be heated by coal, gas, oil or electricity; what matters is that heat is equally distributed and the required temperature is available; an electric oven has a thermostat. A proving chamber is a cabinet with temperature and humidity control used for fermenting bread, rolls and buns. Refrigerators are defrosted weekly and deep freezers at least once a month. Steel or marble work tables are smooth and easy to keep clean; open sides and no drawers are best. One low pressure gas burner is a must in a bakery.
